1:
Delitzsch opens by mapping the chapter onto its parallel: verses 1 through 9 answer to 2 Samuel 5:1-10, and the roll of heroes that follows answers to 2 Samuel 23:8-39. What the chronicler has left out is the seven years between. Delitzsch supplies them: after Saul fell, David came up from Ziklag to Hebron and was anointed over Judah alone, while Abner took Ishbosheth to Mahanaim and made him king over Gilead, and gradually over Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin and the remainder as he won the ground back from the Philistines. Clarke does not retell it at all. He prints a bare outline of the chapter and sends the reader to his notes on 2 Samuel 5, treating the passage as a duplicate already handled.

Ellicott reads the omission as deliberate. The opening word is not "then" but simply "and"; "then" is too definite a mark of time, and the chronicler has passed over the whole decline of Saul's house under a puppet king managed by Abner his powerful kinsman. The phrase "all Israel" then does real work: it proves the election in view is not the anointing by Judah at 2 Samuel 2:4. Hebron, where they gather, is the burial-place of the patriarchs and the capital of David's own tribe. "We are thy bone and thy flesh" Ellicott takes as a proverb that begins in physical kinship (Genesis 2:23) and passes into moral unity (Judges 9:2). The point is that David was no valiant foreigner, as certain of his own heroes were.

The claim of verse 2 rests on service already rendered. "In time past" is literally "yesterday, or three days since", and Ellicott shows how elastic the idiom is: it covers fourteen years at Genesis 31:2 and more than forty at 2 Kings 13:5. To lead out is to lead to battle and to bring in is the homeward march, so David had been discharging the chief kingly function for years without the title. The word rendered "feed" is to shepherd or tend, and Ellicott notes it is used of the Lord himself at Isaiah 40:11. The king is therefore God's representative and his right really divine. Ellicott adds that the cuneiform documents show "shepherd" applied to sovereigns as far back as the pre-Semitic stage of Babylonian civilisation.

On the covenant of verse 3 Ellicott and Henry reach the same conclusion from opposite directions. Ellicott reads it institutionally: the elders are the Senate of Israel, hereditary heads of the tribal subdivisions, and what they make with David is a contract settling the manner of the kingdom, as 1 Samuel 10:25 had provided. Representative institutions, he holds, were the rule in the best period of Israel's national existence. "Before the Lord" means in the presence of the high priest, and perhaps before the ark, since at 1 Samuel 2:25 the priestly judge is himself called God as representing the authority of the divine judge. The closing appeal to the word of the Lord by Samuel he marks as the chronicler's own reflection, added on the basis of 1 Samuel 16:13. Henry reads the same clause morally: between prince and people there is an original contract which both ought religiously to observe. His argument runs from the strongest case. If any prince might have claimed absolute despotic power, and been safely entrusted with it, David might; and David still took the coronation-oath and bound himself to rule by law. Henry also takes the seven years Delitzsch has just narrated as the lesson of the passage rather than an embarrassment to it: God's counsels will be fulfilled at last, whatever difficulties lie in the way, and men who have long stood in their own light may yet be expected to weary of their lying vanities and return to their own mercies.
4:
Ellicott works through the capture by holding the chronicler against Samuel clause by clause. Samuel says only that the king and his men went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land; the chronicler adds the explanatory "that is Jebus" because of the after-mention of the Jebusite, and recasts the sentence so that the Jebusites appear as a settled population. On the name itself Ellicott notes that Jerusalem means city of Salem, that the Hebrew form has been so modified as to suggest "vision of peace", and that in Greek it became Hierosolyma, Sacred Solyma. "Inhabitants of the land" he calls a standing name of the native Canaanites, marking them as indigenous.

"Thou shalt not come hither" Ellicott calls a jeer. Samuel gives it in fuller form, with the boast that the blind and the lame will have kept David out; the Jebusites trusted in the strength of their fortress, and thought even the weakest defence sufficient to repel the assault. At verse 6 the two accounts diverge furthest. Samuel's version, which Ellicott judges obscure but evidently original, has David offer his reward to whoever smites the Jebusite and hurls down the waterfall, the lame and the blind, the hated of David's soul, with the saying about blind and lame not entering the house attached to it. The chronicler appears to have followed another and clearer account, one that makes Joab play at the storm of Jebus the part Othniel played at Kirjath-sepher (Judges 1:12-13). Joab is not mentioned at all in the parallel passage.

What Joab won by it is disputed. Ellicott observes that Joab already appears as David's general while Ishbosheth is yet reigning at Mahanaim, so the promotion can hardly be to a post he already held; he suggests the phrase may mean head and governor of Jerusalem rather than of the army. Wesley takes it nationally: before this Joab was one of David's chief captains, but now he is made captain-general of all the forces of Israel and Judah. Henry is not interested in the office but in what produced the exploit. Opposition quickens resolution, for when the Jebusites set David at defiance he resolved to force the place whatever it cost him; so does the prospect of preferment, and Henry quotes the saying that if you take honour out of the soldier's eye you cut off the spurs from his heels.

On the building Ellicott reads verse 8 as a complete circuit: David started from the Millo, probably a tower or citadel like the Arx Antonia of later times, and brought his line of defences round to it again. Samuel has instead "from the Millo, and inward", which seems to mean the buildings were carried from the fortress towards the interior of the city; Ellicott allows that both statements may of course be true. Delitzsch adds a philological point about what Joab did with the rest of it: the verb means to make alive, and is used here as at Nehemiah 4:2 of the rebuilding of ruins. Verse 9 Ellicott finds corresponds word for word with Samuel, only omitting "God" after "Lord"; literally David walked on, a walking and growing great, a common Hebrew metaphor of gradual and progressive increase, for which he offers the musical term andante. The title Lord of hosts he derives from God's supremacy over the host of heaven, the stars worshipped as deities by the surrounding races, noting that in old Babylonian the very word for God is represented by a star, and that Assur is called in the inscriptions king of the legions of heaven and earth. Delitzsch treats the same verse structurally, as the general remark that opens the way to the register of heroes.
10:
Henry sets the register against the verse before it. David waxed greater and greater, and these were his mighty men; but much of the strength and honour of great men is borrowed from their servants, and take these away and he is where he was. Yet the same verse says the Lord of hosts was with him, so God wrought for him by means and the use of second causes. Wesley puts it in almost the same words, ascribing the success not to the hosts David had but to the Lord of hosts. Henry presses the title of the catalogue too: these are the men who strengthened themselves with him, and in strengthening him they strengthened themselves, since his advancement was theirs. Ellicott reads the same clause as the chronicler's own addition, absent from Samuel.

The register is damaged, and Clarke and Ellicott converge on the damage from different directions. Clarke reproduces Kennicott's finding that about thirty-four Hebrew words have been lost here and are happily preserved in Samuel: the catalogue divides thirty-seven warriors into a captain-general, a first three, a second three and the remaining thirty, and the third captain of the first ternary is missing. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by restoring the lost lines himself, and adds the mechanism. The phrase "the Philistines gathered together" occurs twice, and the eye of a copyist wandered from one to the other. What dropped out was the substance of Eleazar's exploit, that his prowess turned the flight at Pas-dammim into a victory. Ellicott then shows the damage spreading: once the omission was perpetuated, some editor took the singular verbs of Shammah's stand in the barley field for plurals referring to David and Eleazar.

Smaller cruxes follow the same pattern. Whether the field held barley or lentils cannot be settled, Ellicott says, the Hebrew words being very similar. "Saved them" and Samuel's "made a great deliverance" differ by the transposition of one letter. The rock of verse 15 and Samuel's harvest are likewise near-identical in Hebrew, and Ellicott judges the phrase here a correction of the other. On the title "chief of the captains" the Hebrew reads head of the Thirty, and Ellicott suspects even that of standing for head of the Three; Delitzsch defends the reading as the thirty chiefs, against Thenius, who construed the words otherwise.

Over the three hundred slain Ellicott and Wesley divide. Samuel says eight hundred; Ellicott keeps three hundred, arguing that the text in Samuel is otherwise very faulty, though he allows that since Abishai the lesser hero slew three hundred, the greater number may be correct. He is unembarrassed by the figure, comparing the like exploit of Shamgar and observing that a well-armed champion might cut down whole companies of ordinary fighting-men. Wesley harmonises instead: three hundred fell by his own hand and five hundred more by others then joining with him who pursued the victory, the whole slaughter being justly ascribed to him as the effect of his valour. Clarke meanwhile prints the Targum's expansion, in which David sits on the throne of judgment anointed with the holy oil.

On the water of Bethlehem Ellicott is again technical: the three broke through not the main army but the outpost in front of Bethlehem, no such well is now known,and the pouring out uses the term proper to a libation, a free sacrifice under a sudden impulse of thankfulness rather than by prescription of the Law. Henry finds four honourable dispositions in it, and reckons the act as great as any exploit in the chapter: repentance for his own weakness, denial of his own appetite, devotion in giving God what he thought too precious for himself, and tenderness towards his servants, in whose account the water turns to blood. Wesley shares the last, holding it to the honour of great men not to be prodigal of the blood of those they employ.
20:
Abishai's entry is a textual knot from the first word. Ellicott notes the Hebrew here spells him Abshai where Samuel has Abishai, and that "chief of the three" apparently means the second triad, the one whose exploit at the well has just been told. He also notices that the deed credited to Abishai is described in the very words used of Jashobeam: he had brandished his spear over three hundred slain. Where the Hebrew text of Samuel seems to read "knights", some manuscripts, the Hebrew margin and all the versions agree with Chronicles.

Verse 21 then divides the commentators, and each defends the received text against a different proposed emendation. Ellicott treats the Chronicles reading as an exegetical alteration of Samuel's "Above the three, was he not honoured?", and renders it "Above the three of the second rank he was honoured", making Abishai the most honoured member of the second triad; the Vulgate supports him with inter tres secundos inclitus, though the Greek gives "Of the three, renowned above the two". The decisive point for Ellicott is that the Hebrew says literally "in the two", which plainly indicates a second group of three. Delitzsch construes the same phrase quite differently, as honoured before the three as two, that is, doubly honoured, so that he became to them prince and leader; and where Bertheau would alter the word as meaningless to make it correspond with Samuel, Delitzsch defends it on grammatical grounds. Ellicott adds that the Syriac reads thirty for three in both verses, and judges the Arabic more correct. Wesley passes over all of it in four words: he did not equal them.

Delitzsch also supplies the architecture of the list. Because no special deeds are related of the men in verses 26 to 47, he takes them as a third class, below the first triad and below Abishai and Benaiah, subordinate within the royal body-guards. Samuel's roll has thirty-two names which with the three and the two make the thirty-seven expressly remarked at 2 Samuel 23:39; the chronicler states no number and increases the register by sixteen names at the end.

On Benaiah's Egyptian Ellicott works the differences both ways. The chronicler's "a man of measure, five in the cubit" supplies a reason where Samuel says only that he was a man to look at. "Like a weaver's beam" is likewise absent from Samuel, and Ellicott allows it may be due to a recollection of the combat with Goliath, noting that the Greek of the parallel has instead the beam of a ship's ladder, which may be original. But he refuses to let the resemblance become literary: Benaiah's staff is a different Hebrew word from David's, and the similarity of the two accounts, so far as it extends, is a similarity not of fiction but of fact. "Went down" he takes of descending to the combat, comparing the Latin descendere in aciem.

Clarke contributes the Targum twice, and both times it pulls the passage toward the study rather than the field. Benaiah becomes a valiant man fearing sin and of righteous conduct in Kabzeel, who slew two of the nobles of Moab who were like two strong lions, and who, having broken pieces of ice to wash with, went up and read the book of the law of the priests in a short winter's day. At verse 25 the same source makes David's guard into his disciples. Ellicott reads that office in the opposite direction: "over his guard" is literally over his obedience, an abstract for a concrete as at Isaiah 11:14, and what is meant is the Cherethites and Pelethites, a small corps probably of foreigners under David's direct orders. He notes the word carries this precise sense only in this place and its parallel, and that the third member of the second triad is omitted here, as in the case of the first.
26:
Ellicott begins by identifying the list: these warriors are none other than the famous band of thirty already spoken of, and thirty, once the original number, may have become the conventional name of the corps even when its limits had been enlarged. As far as verse 41 the heroes are arranged in pairs, each with his gentilic or cantonal name usually added, and these men belong mostly to Judah and Benjamin. The sixteen additional names that follow are different: so far as they are known they belong to the transjordanic tribes, and the northern tribes are not represented at all.

The break falls at Uriah the Hittite, whose history the chronicler omits. Ellicott notes that the list in Samuel closes with that name and sums itself up as thirty and seven, so the sixteen that follow may indicate a later revision of the catalogue; they are not given elsewhere. Wesley accounts for the same addition substantively rather than editorially: though they were not of the thirty, they were men of great valour and renown amongst David's commanders.

Most of Ellicott's work here is the patient repair of names, and it yields a catalogue of the ways a name decays. Letters fade, so that Samuel's Zalmon may lie behind Ilai. Similar letters are confused, so Sibbecai appears in Samuel as Mebunnai, and d and r change places to give Hiddai for Hurai. A word's last three letters are copied twice and become the word "sons". A place-name hardens into a person: "of Zobah" becomes the improbable Mibhar, and "the Gadite" becomes Haggeri, with the name Bani dropping out between them. The most interesting case is the Pelonite. The Hebrew means simply so-and-so, and Ellicott takes it for a scribe's substitute for an illegible name. When it recurs at verse 36, where Samuel reads Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, he offers two possibilities and declines to choose: either the name had become obscure in the chronicler's manuscript, or the chronicler was unwilling to mention the traitor. He also cannot resist a flyer at verse 26: Dodo is very much like David, so is Elhanan son of Dodo a third alias of the slayer of Goliath?

Delitzsch takes up the last verses, reporting the guesses rather than adjudicating them. For the strange form rendered "the Mahavite" he gives Bertheau's conjecture that it denotes he of Mahanaim in the east-Jordan land; Ellicott independently arrives at the same repair, calling it probably a corruption of the Mahanaimite. For the Mesobaite, which he observes is not in form a clan-name at all, he sets Reland's contraction of Migdal Zebujah, a place the rabbins put near Hebron, against Bertheau's view that the article came into the text by mistake and the remaining consonants recall the form in Samuel. Delitzsch closes that second suggestion with a question mark of his own.

Two disputes remain. At verse 42 Ellicott reads Adina as a captain with thirty men besides him, and reasons that if the thirty were the officers of David's guard of six hundred, each captain would lead about twenty, so Adina's corps is mentioned perhaps as being larger than usual; Wesley reads the same thirty as thirty captains who were under him as their colonel. And on the foreigners Ellicott and Henry agree on the fact and differ on its weight. Ellicott simply observes that many of David's warriors were aliens, instancing Uriah the Hittite, Ittai the Gittite and Ithmah the Moabite. Henry finds a difficulty, since Deuteronomy 23:3 barred the Ammonite and the Moabite from the congregation of the Lord, and concludes that these had approved themselves so hearty for the interest of Israel that it was thought fit to dispense with that law, the rather because it indicated that the Son of David would have worthies among the Gentiles, with whom there is neither Greek nor Jew.
